report:
Your skepticism is justified: the evidence does **not** support the claim that more childhood vaccines increase autism risk.

The strongest direct test of “too many vaccines” is a CDC/NIMH-described *Journal of Pediatrics* study comparing total vaccine-antigen exposure in children with and without autism; it found no association with ASD: https://www.nimh.nih.gov/news/science-updates/2013/autism-risk-unrelated-to-total-vaccine-exposure-in-early-childhood

For MMR specifically, a Danish nationwide cohort of about 657,461 children found MMR vaccination did not increase autism risk, including in higher-risk subgroups: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30831578/

Broader syntheses agree. A meta-analysis of cohort and case-control studies concluded vaccines are not associated with autism: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5789217/ . WHO’s Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety has repeatedly reviewed the issue and again reports evidence from 31 studies (2010–2025) confirming no causal link with ASD: https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/medicines/pharmacovigilance/rev1_vaccines-autism-and-asd-evidence-review-2010-2025_12-dec7ab84d63-5110-4b2c-9882-19651446b8cd.pdf?sfvrsn=daab5374_6

Conclusion: the claim is false. Rising autism diagnoses are better explained by changing definitions, awareness, and ascertainment than by vaccine exposure; the vaccine hypothesis traces to a discredited/retracted 1998 paper and has failed replication in large, controlled studies.
